title: Power On
subtitle: From the power button to your desktop

lines.text: Your Mac is off.
Almost. Somewhere inside, a few tiny circuits are still awake — waiting for a single press.
And when it comes, a cold slab of silicon turns itself into a working computer, in a matter of seconds.
Firmware. Bootloaders. A kernel. Hundreds of programs, each one starting the next.
And not one of them is trusted until it's been checked.
Because whoever controls the very first instruction… controls everything that comes after it.
Today: what really happens when you press the power button.
The press closes a tiny switch, and wakes a power-management chip that never fully sleeps.
It switches on the processor's power supplies one at a time, in a strict order — waiting for each voltage to settle before starting the next.
Get the order wrong, and the chip could misbehave — or even be damaged.
A quartz crystal starts to vibrate — the 24 MHz heartbeat from Episode One — and the clocks lock on.
lines.say: A quartz crystal starts to vibrate — the twenty-four megahertz heartbeat from Episode One — and the clocks lock on.

lines.text: Then the reset signal is released. A single processor core wakes up, knowing exactly one thing: where to find its first instruction.
That instruction lives in the Boot ROM: a small program etched into the chip itself, when it was made. It can never be changed.
lines.say: That instruction lives in the Boot [ROM](/ɹˈɑːm/): a small program etched into the chip itself, when it was made. It can never be changed.

lines.text: That's its strength, and its weakness: if a flaw were ever found in a Boot ROM, no software update could fix it — only a new chip. So it's kept as small and simple as possible.
lines.say: That's its strength, and its weakness: if a flaw were ever found in a Boot [ROM](/ɹˈɑːm/), no software update could fix it — only a new chip. So it's kept as small and simple as possible.

lines.text: Built into it is a key — Apple's public key. Everything that follows is anchored to it.
The Boot ROM's job is to load the next stage, the Low-Level Bootloader, from a small flash chip on the logic board.
lines.say: The Boot [ROM's](/ɹˈɑːmz/) job is to load the next stage, the Low-Level Bootloader, from a small flash chip on the logic board.

lines.text: But before it runs a single instruction of it, the Boot ROM checks its signature.
lines.say: But before it runs a single instruction of it, the Boot [ROM](/ɹˈɑːm/) checks its signature.

lines.text: Here's how. The code is run through a hash function, which boils it down to a short fingerprint.
Change even a single bit, and the fingerprint changes completely.
Apple signs that fingerprint with a private key that never leaves Apple. The public key in the Boot ROM can check the signature — but it can't forge one.
lines.say: Apple signs that fingerprint with a private key that never leaves Apple. The public key in the Boot [ROM](/ɹˈɑːm/) can check the signature — but it can't forge one.

lines.text: If the check fails, the Mac refuses to start, and waits for another computer to restore it.
If it passes, control moves on. And from here on, every stage checks the next one before handing over. A chain of trust, anchored in silicon.
The Low-Level Bootloader starts out in a tiny scratchpad of memory inside the chip — because the main memory isn't ready yet.
It verifies and loads firmware for the chip's helper processors: storage, display, power management, Thunderbolt.
It trains the DRAM — sending test patterns back and forth, fine-tuning the timing until every bit arrives cleanly.
lines.say: It trains the D RAM — sending test patterns back and forth, fine-tuning the timing until every bit arrives cleanly.

lines.text: And it reads the boot policy: a small file, signed by the Secure Enclave, that records the security settings you chose.
That policy is also the only way to start something other than macOS, like Linux: you have to lower the security setting yourself, from recovery, with your password.
Then it hands over to iBoot — the main bootloader, which belongs to the version of macOS you're starting.
iBoot loads a map of all the hardware, called the device tree, and the kernel itself — checking every signature along the way.
Meanwhile, the Secure Enclave boots its own operating system, from its own Boot ROM, walled off from everything else.
lines.say: Meanwhile, the Secure Enclave boots its own operating system, from its own Boot [ROM](/ɹˈɑːm/), walled off from everything else.

lines.text: Finally, iBoot checks the seal on the system volume… and jumps into the kernel.
That seal protects macOS itself. The operating system lives on a read-only volume, where every file has its own hash.
Those hashes are hashed again, and again, all the way up a tree, into a single value: the seal.
Change one byte, in one file, anywhere — and the seal breaks.
And it isn't checked just once. Every time the kernel reads from the system volume, it hashes the data again and compares.
That's why even malware with administrator rights can't quietly rewrite the system. It would break the seal.
Now the kernel is in charge. First, it switches on virtual memory, giving itself — and every future program — its own map of addresses.
It wakes the other processor cores, one by one, and starts the scheduler.
It walks the device tree and matches each piece of hardware with a driver.
Every system program it starts must match a list of approved fingerprints — the trust cache that iBoot loaded and checked.
Then it creates the very first program.
Process number one: launchd. Every other program on your Mac will be its descendant.
lines.say: Process number one: [launchd](/lˈɑːntʃ dˈiː/). Every other program on your Mac will be its descendant.

lines.text: It reads hundreds of small configuration files, and starts the system's background services — logging, networking, Bluetooth, search — many of them only when they're needed.
Within seconds, hundreds of processes are running — before you've even logged in.
One of them is the WindowServer, which takes over the display. Another is the login window.
lines.say: One of them is the Window Server, which takes over the display. Another is the login window.

lines.text: You type your password. Your Mac never stores the password itself.
With FileVault on, the Secure Enclave combines it with a secret key fused into this one chip, to unlock the keys that protect your data.
Your files were encrypted the whole time. Now they can be read.
launchd starts your session: the menu bar, the Dock, the Finder… and your desktop.
lines.say: [launchd](/lˈɑːntʃ dˈiː/) starts your session: the menu bar, the Dock, the Finder… and your desktop.

lines.text: So, from the top.

A press. Power, in sequence. A crystal, a clock, a single core. The Boot ROM checks the bootloader. The bootloader checks iBoot. iBoot checks the kernel. The kernel checks every system file it reads. launchd. The login window. You.
lines.say: A press. Power, in sequence. A crystal, a clock, a single core. The Boot [ROM](/ɹˈɑːm/) checks the bootloader. The bootloader checks iBoot. iBoot checks the kernel. The kernel checks every system file it reads. [launchd](/lˈɑːntʃ dˈiː/). The login window. You.

lines.text: Every link verified before it runs. A chain of trust, forged from scratch, every time you press that button.
Next time: memory. Where does all this data actually live — and how does the chip get to it so fast?
